Egypt Faces Escalating Currency Crisis as Pound Plummets

Cairo—Egypt is grappling with a deepening currency crisis as the Egyptian pound continues its steep decline, sending shockwaves through businesses and households nationwide. The pound has lost nearly 50% of its value against the US dollar since the beginning of the year, with the official exchange rate reaching a record 62 EGP per dollar on Tuesday. Black market rates have soared even higher, further eroding confidence in the local currency.

The Central Bank of Egypt has imposed stringent capital controls and raised interest rates in an attempt to stem the outflow of foreign currency. However, these measures have so far failed to stabilize the market, as importers struggle to secure dollars and inflation accelerates. Official inflation figures released this week showed annual consumer price inflation climbing to 37% in May, its highest level in decades.

“The current crisis is unprecedented in recent years, and the impact is being felt across every sector of the economy,” said Dr. Hala Mostafa, senior economist at the Cairo Institute for Economic Studies. “Businesses can’t plan beyond the short term, and many are reducing operations or laying off staff.”

The crisis has hit import-dependent industries particularly hard. At Port Said, containers are piling up as importers cannot pay suppliers abroad. The Federation of Egyptian Industries reports that 40% of manufacturers are operating below half capacity due to shortages of raw materials. “Our production lines are idle while we wait for foreign currency,” said Ahmed El-Sayed, general manager at Nile Textiles. “We’ve had to furlough a third of our staff.”

Ordinary Egyptians are also feeling the pinch. Prices of staple foods such as bread, rice, and cooking oil have doubled since January. Many families are cutting back on meals or turning to government-subsidized outlets, where supplies are increasingly rationed.

Finance Minister Mohamed Anwar told reporters on Tuesday that the government is in talks with international lenders for emergency assistance. “We are committed to stabilizing the currency and protecting the most vulnerable,” he said. However, analysts warn that, without significant foreign inflows or structural reforms, further turbulence is likely in the months ahead.
